```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
# Show a file from a bundled example, as it ships with the package.
example_file <- function(...) system.file("examples", ..., package = "spigot", mustWork = TRUE)
```

spigot lets you build a Shiny app the way you would build a small website: pages are
hand-written HTML and JavaScript, and the server side is a set of
[plumber](https://www.rplumber.io/) endpoints. spigot mounts the plumber router inside the
Shiny app, so the pages and the API share one process, one origin and one port. Shiny still
hosts the app (locally, on Shiny Server or on Posit Connect), gives each browser tab a
session, and keeps a websocket open to it.

```
Browser tab ──HTTP fetch──▶ /api/*  ──▶ plumber router ─┐
     ▲                                                  │ same R process,
     │                                                  │ same memory
     └──websocket (Shiny session)◀── observers/push ◀───┘
```

The API is for the app's own pages, not for other clients. By default it answers only
requests that carry the session token of an open tab of the app.

This vignette walks through two of the examples that ship with spigot: `minimal`, one page
and four endpoints, and `site`, a three-page site with shared templates and an endpoint that
runs its work in another process. `vignette("reactivity", package = "spigot")` covers the
third example, `live`, and pushing data to pages.

## Installation

```r
# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("kent-orr/spigot")
```

Run any example with `run_example()`:

```r
spigot::run_example("minimal")
```

## The minimal example

An app is a folder with an `app.R`. The `minimal` example's folder holds:

```
minimal/
├── app.R        # spigot_app(): the page and the API
├── api.R        # plumber endpoints, served under /api
├── index.html   # the page
└── www/         # files served as they are
    ├── app.js
    └── style.css
```

### `app.R`

```{embed, file = example_file("minimal", "app.R")}
```

`spigot_app()` returns an ordinary Shiny app object, so `shiny::runApp("minimal")`,
Shiny Server and Posit Connect all run the folder like any other app (see
[Running the app](#running)). Its arguments:

* `pages`: one page, served at `/`, or a named list of pages keyed by path.
* `api`: a plumber file, or a router you built in code with `spigot_api()`.
* `prefix`: where the API is mounted; `"/api"` by default.
* `server`: an optional Shiny server function, for push and reactivity.
* `require_session`: `TRUE` by default; see [Sessions](#sessions) below.

### Running the app {#running}

Run the app's folder:

```r
shiny::runApp("minimal")   # or shiny::runApp("minimal/app.R")
```

RStudio's Run App button, Shiny Server, Posit Connect and `run_example()` do the same.
Shiny loads any `.R` files in the folder's `R/` subfolder, sources `app.R` from inside the
folder, serves `www/`, and keeps the folder as the working directory while the app runs.

Running the app *object* is different. Printing the object `spigot_app()` returns runs it,
and that happens at the console, when `app.R` is sourced with echo, and with
`Rscript app.R`. Shiny then does none of the above:

|                                              | `runApp("minimal")` | the printed object                    |
|----------------------------------------------|---------------------|---------------------------------------|
| `spigot_page("index.html")`, `api = "api.R"` | read from the folder | read from the working directory, an error if they are not there |
| files in `www/`                              | served              | `404`                                 |
| functions in `R/`                            | loaded              | not loaded                            |

So a page's `<script src="app.js">` gets spigot's HTML 404 page, which the browser refuses
to run ("blocked due to MIME type"), and an endpoint that calls a function from `R/` fails
with a `500`. From a terminal, use `Rscript -e 'shiny::runApp("minimal")'`. An app that
keeps its page and API in one script, like the one in the README, reads no files and
runs either way.

### `api.R`: the endpoints

`api.R` is a plain plumber file. Annotate a function with `#* @get /path` (or `@post`,
`@put`, `@delete`), and its arguments come from the query string and the JSON body.

```{embed, file = example_file("minimal", "api.R")}
```

Replies are JSON, serialised by `spigot_json()`: length-1 vectors become scalars, `NA`
becomes `null`, and a data frame becomes an array of row objects. Wrap a value in `I()` to
keep a length-1 vector as an array. Setting `res$status` sends another status code, and the
page's code can read the JSON body of the error.

Request bodies are parsed by plumber as usual: JSON, forms and multipart uploads. For a
binary body, such as a file sent as a `Blob`, give the endpoint `#* @parser octet`;
plumber's default parsers would try to read it as text.

### `index.html`: the page

`spigot_page("index.html")` reads a complete HTML document. spigot adds jQuery, Shiny's
JavaScript and `spigot.js` to its `<head>` when it serves the page, so the template needs no
script tags for them. It needs only a `</head>` tag, and loads its own files from `www/`
with relative URLs (`style.css`, `app.js`).

The template is a [whisker](https://github.com/edwindj/whisker) (Mustache) template; `data`
fills it in. The minimal page has no `{{ }}` tags; the `site` example below uses them.

### `www/app.js`: calling the API

`spigot.js` defines `spigot.get()`, `spigot.post()`, `spigot.put()` and `spigot.del()`.
Paths are relative to the API, so `spigot.get("hello", {name: "Ada"})` requests
`api/hello?name=Ada` relative to the page, which keeps working when the app is served under a
subpath. Each call returns a promise of the parsed JSON reply:

```js
const reply = await spigot.get("hello", { name: "Ada" });
reply.message;   // "Hello, Ada!"

try {
  await spigot.get("summary", { n: 0 });
} catch (err) {
  // A non-2xx reply, or no reply at all (err.status is then 0).
  err.status;    // 400
  err.message;   // "n must be a whole number from 1 to 100000": the JSON `error` field
  err.body;      // the whole parsed reply
}
```

The example's page script wraps these calls to show each outcome:

```{embed, file = example_file("minimal", "www", "app.js")}
```

`vignette("client", package = "spigot")` documents the whole client.

### Sessions {#sessions}

Each browser tab is a Shiny session. `spigot.js` waits for it to start, then sends its token
with every request in an `X-Spigot-Session` header, and spigot binds the request to that
session. An endpoint gets the session with `spigot_session(req)`, and can keep per-tab state
in `session$userData`:

```r
#* @get /visits
function(req) {
  s <- spigot::spigot_session(req)
  s$userData$visits <- sum(s$userData$visits, 1)
  list(visits = s$userData$visits)
}
```

With `require_session = TRUE`, the default, a request without the token of an open tab gets
a `401`, so `curl` and other sites cannot call the API. Use `require_session = FALSE` for an
API that should also answer those requests; `spigot_session()` then returns `NULL` for them.
Whatever the setting, requests from pages on another origin get a `403`.

## The site example

`site` is a small site about R's `mtcars` data with three pages: a home page, a table of the
cars, and a page that fits a regression. It shows templates with data, shared partials,
blueprints, and an endpoint whose work runs in another R process.

```
site/
├── app.R
├── api.R
├── R/                  # loaded by Shiny before app.R
│   ├── data.R          # the data, and a page() helper
│   ├── pages-cars.R    # the cars blueprint
│   └── pages-model.R   # the model blueprint
├── templates/
│   ├── index.html
│   ├── partials/       # shared by every page
│   │   ├── head.html
│   │   ├── nav.html
│   │   └── footer.html
│   ├── cars/cars.html
│   └── model/model.html
└── static/
    ├── site.css
    ├── cars/cars.js
    └── model/model.js
```

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "app.R")}
```

`templates`, `partials` and `static` say where the files are; the `/cars` and `/model`
sections are blueprints, each with its own templates and static files:

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "R", "pages-cars.R")}
```

`vignette("flask-flow", package = "spigot")` explains this layout.

### Several pages

`pages` is a named list keyed by path. A request for `/cars/` is redirected to `/cars`, and
a path that is neither a page nor a static file gets a 404 page. Pages can also be nested
(`"/docs/intro"`); see `?spigot_page` for how their relative URLs resolve.

A top-level page can also be any Shiny UI, such as a `fluidPage()`, so a classic Shiny page
can sit next to hand-written ones.

### Templates, data and partials

Each page's `data` is a list for its template. `{{title}}` inserts a value with HTML
escaped, so data can never inject markup or R code, `{{#rows}} ... {{/rows}}` repeats for
each element of a list, and `{{> nav}}` inserts a partial. Here is the cars page, which R
renders with all 32 rows:

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "templates", "cars", "cars.html")}
```

Its script is `<script src="{{static}}/cars.js">`: a blueprint's pages get `{{static}}`, the
path its static files are served at (`cars/static`).

All three pages share the `head`, `nav` and `footer` partials from `templates/partials/`. The nav marks the current
page with `aria-current`, using the `page` value each page's data sets:

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "templates", "partials", "nav.html")}
```

`data` can also be a function of the request, called for each request (for example, to read
the query string). The site's data never changes, so its pages use `cache = TRUE` and are
rendered once.

### Server-rendered first, then the API

The cars page arrives with every row already in the HTML. Its filter form then asks the API
for the matching rows and redraws the table body, building elements with `textContent`
rather than HTML strings:

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "static", "cars", "cars.js")}
```

### Slow work: `future_promise()`

R runs one thing at a time. While an endpoint runs, the app serves no other request and no
other tab, so anything slower than about a tenth of a second should not run in the app's R
process. An endpoint can return a promise instead, and spigot replies when it resolves. The
fit endpoint hands its work to a [future](https://future.futureverse.org/) worker with
`promises::future_promise()`:

```{embed, file = example_file("site", "api.R")}
```

`app.R` starts the workers with `future::plan(future::multisession, workers = 2)`. The
worker is another R process: send it the data it needs, as `data` is here, and keep sessions,
`spigot_emit()` and other app state in the main process. To push from a worker's result, do
it in the promise's `then()`. `vignette("reactivity", package = "spigot")` has more on this.

## Deploying

A spigot app is a Shiny app: deploy its folder as you would any other. Some things to know:

* **Subpaths.** Use relative URLs in pages (`href="cars"`, `src="logo.png"`); `spigot.get()`
  and friends already resolve their paths relative to the page. Apps then work under a
  subpath such as `https://example.com/apps/site/`.
* **Request size.** Shiny rejects request bodies larger than
  `getOption("shiny.maxRequestSize")`, 5 MB by default, before any R code runs. That `413`
  reply is plain text, not JSON. Raise the limit with `spigot_app(max_request_size =)`.
* **Several R processes.** Each R process has its own memory and its own sessions. If the
  server runs several processes for one app (Posit Connect can), state kept in R and
  `spigot_broadcast()` reach only the tabs served by the same process.
* **Proxies.** The cross-origin check compares the request's `Origin` with its `Host`, or
  with `X-Forwarded-Host` when a proxy sets it. A proxy that rewrites `Host` without
  setting `X-Forwarded-Host` makes every `POST` from the browser fail with `403`.
